entry.dc:title: PLANNING OF A NEW SURFACE MINE - WESTERN COAL.
entry.dc:creator: Graham R.J.
entry.dc:description: There are five geological provinces in the western states from which 100 percent of the lignite and sub-bituminous coal comes. Part of just one province, the Northern Great Plains, has recoverable reserves of lignite and sub-bituminous and bituminous coal which account for 44 percent of the nation's total. Most of western coal is low in sulfur and, therefore, in demand by utilities who must comply with the Clean Air Act. It lies in thick seams appropriate to surface mining methods. With a majority of coal reserves available in the West, several new mines are in planning stages. The article looks briefly at some of the aspects of mine planning which must be considered.

entry.dc:title: TOUGH STRIP MINING STATUTE IS ASSURED.
entry.dc:creator: Poe E.
entry.dc:description: It is generally agreed that a strict Federal surface mining law will soon become reality. The author attempts to assess the consequential impact of the proposed strip mining statute on the U. S. coal industry, and discusses some of the pertinent provisions of the scheduled new law, as first approved on the House side of the Capital. This surface mining legislation sets minimum standards to be followed by the states in setting up mandatory strip mining control programs.

entry.dc:title: KNIFE RIVER KEEPS AHEAD IN RECLAMATION.
entry.dc:creator: Anon
entry.dc:description: Knife River Coal Co. 's land reclamation efforts at its Beulah, N. D. , mine are highlighted. The company has been leveling spoil piles left by surface mining starting seven years previous to any North Dakota law which required reclamation of mined land. The Beulah mine now has between 200 and 300 acres restored for use as farm land. Scrapers are used to return the topsoil over the leveled spoil material.

entry.dc:title: MINING ENGINEERING'S ANNUAL REVIEW OF COAL AND INDUSTRIAL MINERALS - 1.
entry.dc:creator: Saperstein L.W.
entry.dc:description: Six-part review contains articles on surface mining, underground mining, coal preparation, coal utilization, health and safety, and research and development.

entry.dc:title: SPACE PHOTOGRAPHY-A VALUABLE TOOL FOR SURFACE MINE PLANNING.
entry.dc:creator: Brumbaugh F.
entry.dc:description: Three Skylab investigators have concluded after a study of surface mine area photographic imagery that much can be gained from this medium when used to monitor surface mining and reclamation activities. Given the ever-increasing demand for coal, improved means are needed for the overall planning, management and enforcement of laws governing the surface coal mining industry. Space photography is discussed as one new tool that can help the surface coal mining industry meet these needs. The Skylab findings are detailed.

entry.dc:title: MULTI-SEAM SURFACE MINING IN WEST.
entry.dc:creator: Jackson D.
entry.dc:description: While some Western U. S. coal mining companies have been surface-mining multiple coal seams for some time, others, now planning to use this type of mining, will have to face some new and more complicated problems. The author discusses the use of computers and plotters for spoil diagramming, the sequencing of mining equipment in a multi-seam operation, as well as drilling, blasting and coal handling.

entry.dc:title: UNDERGROUND MINING REVIEW.
entry.dc:creator: Beattie G.
entry.dc:description: Underground mining will soon be called upon for increased production to meet the world's demand for minerals. Adaptation of surface mining techniques has improved underground productivity significantly. The ability to improve mines which are unable to reduce their labor intensive methods still exists. However, dramatic increases in the cost of energy are upsetting the energy, capital, labor relationships. This situation increases the importance of research work directed toward development of continuous mining methods to replace the cyclical method so long in use in the underground hard rock industry. The impact of the labor shortage in mining will continue to increase in severity.

entry.dc:title: SURFACE COAL MINING - 1976.
entry.dc:creator: Eadie G.
entry.dc:description: Although no radically new piece of equipment was developed during 1976 that will change the surface mining industry, there are several experiments of interest. The environmental clout has generated interest in reclamation equipment development. The handling of topsoil has taken a new dimension for many operators who have needed help in meeting legal reclamation requirements. Purchase lead time required has been reduced for equipment. The technology advances in surface mining in 1976 were those brought about by the pressure of production demands.

entry.dc:title: COAL MINING.
entry.dc:creator: Anon
entry.dc:description: Coal mining is presently one of the most hazardous industries in the United States, although vast improvements have occurred in recent years through research, improved equipment design, and mining techniques, inspection, education and training. Accident rates have decreased markedly in areas where workers are aware of the hazards and where they are trained to recognize and control the hazardous conditions. Although many mines now have safety records that are equal to those found in other industries, an all-out effort is underway to further improve the work environment of America's miners. Both underground and surface mining are discussed.

entry.dc:title: FABRICATION OF LARGE SURFACE MINING MACHINERY.
entry.dc:creator: Learmont T.
entry.dc:description: Semi-automatic welding in the shop and manual welding in the field play a major role in fabricating wheel excavators, stripping shovels and walking draglines. Flux cored arc welding, with and without gas shielding, is employed extensively.

entry.dc:title: COAL SURFACE MINING RECLAMATION COSTS IN THE WESTERN UNITED STATES.
entry.dc:creator: Persse F.H.
entry.dc:description: The Bureau of Mines estimated reclamation costs for 13 surface coal mines in nine States west of the Mississippi River. With the exception of the Pacific Coast coal province, at least one mine in each of the western coal provinces was studied. Estimated costs are presented in four categories which represent the four phases of mined-land reclamation: (1) Design, engineering, and overhead; (2) bond and permit fees; (3) backfillling and grading; and (4) revegetation. Total reclamation costs ranged from 860 to 7,200 per acre, from 6 to 84 cents per ton, and from 4 to 35. 3 mills per million Btu. A mine in the NOrthern Great Plains coal province (Region D) showed the highest per acre cost whereas mines in part of the western region of the Interior coal province (Region A) experienced the greatest per ton and per million Btu cost.

entry.dc:title: Mining Exhibition report.
entry.dc:description: A survey of some of the hydraulic equipment for use in all types of mining extraction covering both underground and surface mining that was exhibited at the International Mining Exhibition, U.K. in October 1977.

entry.dc:title: Radiation exposures associated with surface mining for uranium
entry.dc:creator: Miller H.
entry.dc:description: Measurements of external gamma radiation, radon and radon progeny, and airborne uranium aerosols were made at an operating open-pit mining operation using readily available field survey techniques and instruments. Measurement techniques are discussed. Radiation exposure to various occupational categories, such as excavation equipment operators, truck drivers, equipment maintenance personnel, ore control personnel, and to the engineering staff, is estimated. These estimates are compared to the results of film badge dosimetry. While the average exposure rate was found to be in the order of 0.5 mR/hr±0.5 mR/hr, it was noted that higher exposures (up to lOmR/hr) were measured in the vicinity of ore bodies containing uranium in the per cent range. Some contamination of earth-moving equipment by uranium-bearing dusts was also noted. © 1977 Health Physics Society.

entry.dc:title: STRIP MINING OF COAL: ENVIRONMENTAL SOLUTIONS.
entry.dc:creator: Doyle W.S.
entry.prism:publicationName: Strip Min of Coal Environ Solutions
entry.dc:description: In the past strip mining was generally conducted with little regard for its effect on the environment. This has resulted in erosion and water pollution and left areas esthetically scarred and unusable for agriculture, grazing or recreational use. This book, based on 19 government reports issued from 1967 through 1974, describes coal surface mining land use and methods, land reclamation methods and sediment and erosion control. Acid mine drainage, its sources, prevention and correction as well as the mechanism of recovery of acid strip mine lakes are discussed. Specific studies on revegetation, use of spoil amendments and the effects of acid mine drainage are included. One chapter describes the Federal Republic of Germany's approach to the problem of reclamation of strip mined lands. The final two chapters discuss reclamation costs. A complete list of the cited reports is given at the end of the book. This is followed by a list of state agencies to be contacted regarding strip mining and land reclamation.

entry.dc:title: STEMMING THE SLIDE IN PRODUCTIVITY IS A JOB FOR BOTH MACHINERY MANUFACTURER AND MINE OPERATOR.
entry.dc:creator: Anon
entry.dc:description: A survey is presented of some of the new equipment and new techniques available from U. S. and British manufacturers that could help raise the productivity of U. S. coal mines. Longwall mining, the backbone of underground coal mining in Europe, will see a solid growth in the U. S. in the years ahead. In surface mining, there appears to be no new factor in the immediate future that could produce a spectacular increase in output. New equipment and methods focus on the following areas of technical interest: Use of shield supports, particularly in soft floors; application of NCB/Dosco In-Seam Miner; nucleonic sensing devices for longwall shearers; underground communication systems; dust control for longwall machines; and instrumentation techniques for strata control.

entry.dc:title: LAND AND NATURAL RESOURCE INFORMATION AND SOME POTENTIAL ENVIRONMENTAL EFFECTS OF SURFACE MINING OF COAL IN THE GILLETTE AREA, WYOMING.
entry.dc:creator: Keefer W.R.
entry.dc:description: An integrated program of geologic, hydrologic, geochemical, and related studies by the U. S. Geological Survey in central Campbell County provides basic information about the land and its resources, including characteristics of the landscape, properties of rocks and surface materials, depth and thickness of coal, streamflow, depth to ground water, quality of ground water, sediment yield, concentrations of trace elements in soils, rocks, coal, vegetation, and water, and current land use. The data are used to analyze and predict some of the potential environmental effects of surface mining, such as the extent of land disturbance, nature and degree of landscape modification, and disruption of surface-water and ground-water systems. Refs.

entry.dc:title: COAL RESERVES IN MARYLAND - POTENTIAL FOR FUTURE DEVELOPMENT.
entry.dc:creator: Weaver K.N.
entry.dc:description: After a brief historical review of coal development in Maryland, the authors discuss in detail the five coal basins of western Maryland, which include 11 commercially exploitable coal seams. The estimates of the recoverable reserves in each of the five basins are given, and the potential for future coal development is assessed. The total recoverable coal reserves for western Maryland are put at 854,900,000 tons of coal having fairly high BTU and sulfur content. Of this total, an estimated 100 million tons could be recovered by surface mining methods.

entry.dc:title: REHABILITATION OF MINING AREAS WITH PARTICULAR REFERENCE TO THE RE-ESTABLISHMENT OF PLANT GROWTH.
entry.dc:creator: Lothian T.
entry.prism:publicationName: Pap Presented at the Semin on Landscaping and Land Use Plann as Relat to Min Oper
entry.dc:description: Plant growth is likely to prove the most suitable and satisfactory material to stabilize and cover quarry faces and worked-out surface mining sites. The careful selection of plant species is of paramount importance to the success of any attempts to revegetate these sites. Various techniques are recommended and attention is drawn to different factors which will adversely affect plant growth.

entry.dc:title: GUIDE TO STATE PROGRAMS FOR THE RECLAMATION OF SURFACE MINED AREAS.
entry.dc:creator: Imhoff E.
entry.dc:description: During 1975 inquiries of agencies in each State and review of State statutes and related administrative codes revealed that 38 States have established programs requiring the reclamation of surface mined lands. Results of analyses of these programs and ancillary data are presented in: a table (matrix) which has been designed for the notation and elaboration of information pertaining to the mined-area reclamation programs of the 50 States; a primer on surface mining activities and related reclamation practices and problems; and a listing of types of non-Federal governmental controls applicable to reclamation. A general trend is seen in State programs toward the requiring of an integration of land-use planning and nine planning, with increased local governmental involvement. Refs.

entry.dc:title: TYRES FOR THE MINING INDUSTRY.
entry.dc:creator: Anon
entry.dc:description: The manufacture of pneumatic tires for mobile vehicles used in underground and surface mining operations poses many specialized problems and challenges. Equally, operators have developed many systems and techniques to reduce tire costs and optimize productivity with safety. Examined in this article are the applications of rubber technology to heavy earthmover tires, such as those used on large capacity haulage trucks, wheeled loaders and bulldozers. The information is chiefly derived from visits and discussions with many of the major tire companies supplying the mining industry, but open pit and underground operations worldwide have also contributed part of the information.

entry.dc:title: HYDRAULIC MINING AT KAISER RESOURCES UNLOCKS NEW COAL SEAMS.
entry.dc:creator: Overend M.
entry.dc:description: Within five years, Kaiser Resources Limited, at Sparwood, B. C. , has turned a 32 million accumulated loss into a 71 million profit in 1975. The Sparwood operation is a combination of surface mining, conventional underground mining, and a new development in underground technology, hydraulic mining. Production is about 6 one-half million tons of metallurgical coal a year, most of which is sold under long term contracts to Japan. The balance goes to Eastern Canada, Korea, Mexico and Italy.

entry.dc:title: TIMELY MASSEY PURCHASE GETS ST. JOE INTO COAL.
entry.dc:creator: Anon
entry.dc:description: This article describes St. Joe Minerals Corp. 's acquisition and subsequent modernization and expansion of A. T. Massey Coal Co. Massey's production has grown from 4. 9 million tons in 1971 to 9. 2 million in 1975 and is projected at 16 million tons in 1980. The company will continue to broker an additional 5 to 6 million tons of coal annually. Over one-third of Massey's production and two-thirds of the brokered coal is low and medium-volatile coking coal. Less than 20% of Massey's production comes from surface mining. The operations of the coal preparation facilities are also discussed.

entry.dc:title: The effect of coal surface mining on the water quality of mountain drainage basin streams
entry.dc:creator: Minear R.A.
entry.prism:publicationName: Journal of the Water Pollution Control Federation
entry.dc:description: Six small watersheds ranging from 1.7 to 11 sq km (0.7 to 4.3 sq mi) within the New River Basin of the Cumberland mountains of Northern Tennessee have been monitored weekly and simultaneously for water quality between January and December 1975. Three watersheds were undisturbed by mining activity and served to establish bench mark data. The other three watersheds represented varying stages of coal mining activity, ranging from initiation of surface mining in one watershed to essentially complete stripping three years ago and current deep mining activity in another. Distinct differences are observed for the variables pH, alkalinity, sulfate, calcium, magnesium, iron manganese, total solids, and suspended solids among the disturbed watersheds. In contrast to the undisturbed watershed stream constituent concentrations which were quite uniform from stream to stream and from sample to sample.

entry.dc:title: REGIONAL ASPECTS AFFECT PLANNING OF SURFACE MINING OPERATIONS.
entry.dc:creator: Anon
entry.dc:description: Conventional stripping methods are giving way to more sophisticated operational planning as mining costs and environmental regulations continue to grow. This article reviews certain specific improved mining techniques employed by the coal industry in four distinct regions of the United States. Region I was conventional contour mining methods, haulback or lateral movement operations, mountain-top removal, longwall stripping and multi-seam mining. Region II chiefly relies on box-cut contour mining, modified block-cut and block-area mining. Region III uses modified area mining, tandem-dragline operations and bucket wheel operations, while Region IV employs area mining, open pit mining and steeply dipping multi-seams.

entry.dc:title: Overview of international health safety extraction research and development in coal mining
entry.dc:creator: Yancik J.
entry.dc:description: The major coal producing countries have a long history of research efforts directed toward improving coal mining techniques and equipment and improving ways to protect the miners from health and safety hazards. These R&D efforts for the most part concentrate on underground mining, where the magnitude and degree of exposure to hazards are many times greater than in surface mining. Most of the major R&D institutes are listed and pertinent information, where known, is given as to their size, programs and funding. The data is from personal contacts and the Bureau's mining research files unless otherwise noted. A brief discussion of R&D efforts in the top six coal producing countries accompanies the table.
